title: City of West Covina v. Perkins (1999)
shortTitle: City of West Covina v. Perkins (1999)
summary: When police lawfully seize property under a warrant, due process requires notice that the property was taken but not individualized notice of the state law remedies for getting it back.
notes:
Key line: "When the police seize property for a criminal investigation, however, due process does not require them to provide the owner with notice of state-law remedies." (Kennedy, J.)

Citation: 525 U.S. 234 (1999).

sections.Parties: The petitioner was the city of West Covina, California, whose police officers had seized property from a private home while executing a search warrant. The respondents were Lawrence Perkins and members of his family, who owned the home and the property seized. The suspect in the underlying homicide investigation, Marcus Marsh, had been a boarder in the Perkins home and was not a party. The Perkins family sued the city and the officers under 42 U.S.C. section 1983, and the dispute that reached the Supreme Court concerned only the adequacy of the notice the city gave about how to recover the seized property.
sections.Material Facts: On May 20, 1993, a Citrus Municipal Court judge issued a warrant to search the Perkins home for evidence against Marcus Marsh, a former boarder who had become a homicide suspect. On May 21, 1993, West Covina police searched the house and seized photographs of Marsh, an address book, a 12 gauge shotgun, a starter pistol, ammunition and $2,629 in cash. They left a form headed Search Warrant: Notice of Service giving the dates of the warrant and search, the issuing judge and court, and the names and telephone numbers of two detectives and a lieutenant, plus an itemized list of the property. They omitted the warrant number because the warrant was sealed, although the clerk's public index recorded it by address. Perkins telephoned a detective and was told he needed a court order. A month later he went to the courthouse, found the issuing judge on vacation, and was told nothing was filed under his name.
sections.Procedural History: The Perkins family sued in the United States District Court for the Central District of California, alleging Fourth Amendment violations and a city policy permitting unlawful searches. The district court granted summary judgment to the city and officers but invited briefing on a due process question the plaintiffs had not raised. On appeal the Ninth Circuit remanded that question. On remand the district court held that California's remedies for return of seized property satisfied due process and found no evidence that the warrant number was needed to invoke them. The Ninth Circuit reversed, 113 F.3d 1004 (1997), holding by analogy to Memphis Light that the city had to give notice of the procedures for return of the property, including the warrant number or a means of finding the court file. The Supreme Court granted certiorari, 523 U.S. 1105 (1998), and reversed on January 13, 1999.
sections.Issue: Whether the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment requires a state or local government, after lawfully seizing property under a search warrant that it no longer needs for investigation or prosecution, to give the owner detailed and specific notice of the state law procedures for seeking return of the property and of the information needed to invoke them, such as the search warrant number, or whether notice of the seizure itself, combined with published and generally available remedies, satisfies the Constitution.
sections.Holding: The Court held that when police seize property for a criminal investigation, due process does not require them to provide the owner with notice of state law remedies. Individualized notice that the property has been taken is required so that the owner can pursue available remedies, and the city had given that notice along with an inventory. But no similar rationale supports notice of remedies established by published, generally available statutes and case law, which an owner can consult once told of the seizure. The Ninth Circuit's expansive notice requirement lacked support in precedent and conflicted with the practice of the federal government and all fifty states. The judgment was reversed.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Kennedy explained that the purpose of notice under the Due Process Clause is to make the opportunity for a hearing meaningful. Notice of the seizure is necessary because the owner otherwise has no reasonable way to learn who took his property. Once informed, he can turn to public sources such as California Penal Code sections 1536 and 1540 to learn the remedial procedures, as Reetz v. Michigan and Atkins v. Parker recognized in analogous settings. Memphis Light was different: there the utility's dispute procedure was not described in any publicly available document and depended on word of mouth, so a customer could not educate himself about it. The case did not establish a general rule that government must give notice of remedies. The Court stressed that Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 41(d) and every state's search warrant statute require only a copy of the warrant and a receipt or inventory, so sustaining the Ninth Circuit would have made every such provision constitutionally inadequate. The Court also rejected the narrower argument that the notice was deficient for omitting the warrant number, because the district court had found no evidence that the number was needed to obtain a court order releasing property identified by date, agency, officer and issuing judge.

topics.lrs-o-due-process-framework: The opinion separates notice of seizure from an individualized description of recovery procedures already published in statute.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Kennedy's opinion was joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. Justice Thomas, joined by Justice Scalia, concurred in the judgment. He agreed that the city need not give detailed notice of postdeprivation remedies but refused to endorse the majority's statement that due process requires officers executing a warrant to take reasonable steps to give notice that property has been taken, arguing that the Fourth Amendment, informed by the common law practice of furnishing an inventory of goods seized, rather than procedural due process, governs the execution of criminal search warrants.
